issues.legal_issue: Prior environmental clearance for a national highway expansion exceeding the specified length is required only when the additional right of way or land acquisition also exceeds the applicable width limit.
material_facts: The highway expansion covered 179.555 kilometres and was divided into four packages, each shorter than 100 kilometres.
No environmental impact assessment had been undertaken.
The additional land acquisition was not greater than 40 metres on existing alignments or 60 metres on realignments or bypasses.
issues.conclusion: Prior environmental clearance was not required for the project because, although the overall expansion exceeded 100 kilometres, the additional land acquisition did not exceed the applicable width limits.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 3(2)(v) of the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 and Rules 5 of the Environment (Protection) Rules, 1986, the 2006 Environmental Impact Assessment Notification, as amended in 2013, requires clearance for a national highway expansion exceeding 100 kilometres only if the additional right of way or land acquisition exceeds 40 metres on existing alignments or 60 metres on realignments or bypasses. The Court applied the ordinary, literal meaning of clear and unambiguous text, treating a notification as subordinate legislation to be construed like statutory text. It relied on State of Tamil Nadu v. Hind Stone, State of Uttar Pradesh v. Babu Ram Upadhya, Bansal Wire Industries Ltd. v. State of U.P., Sussex Peerage case, Dental Council of India v. Hari Prakash, Harbhajan Singh v. Press Council of India, South Central Railway Employees Coop. Credit Society Employees’ Union v. Registrar of Coop. Societies, and CIT v. Surat Art Silk Cloth Manufacturers’ Association; it also accepted the notification-authoring ministry’s interpretation, referring to Silppi Construction Contractors v. Union of India.

predicates.national_highway_expansion_project: The project proponent undertook an expansion of a national highway.
predicates.project_exceeds_100_km: The overall highway expansion exceeded 100 kilometres.
predicates.land_acquisition_within_alignment_limit: The additional right of way or land acquisition did not exceed the applicable width limit for the alignment.

issues.definition: When a national highway expansion exceeds 100 kilometres but its additional land acquisition remains within the applicable alignment limit, prior environmental clearance is not required.

issues.legal_issue: Dividing a national highway project into shorter packages as a strategy to avoid environmental clearance is impermissible, although whether segmentation is permissible in other circumstances requires expert examination.
material_facts: The overall project extended 179.555 kilometres and was divided into four packages, each shorter than 100 kilometres.
The project proponent relied on administrative and execution needs, including the difficulty of engaging one concessionaire and the need for speedy completion.
The Court considered that allowing segmentation to avoid clearance would undermine the notification’s environmental-clearance requirements.
issues.conclusion: Segmentation cannot be used as a strategy to evade environmental clearance. The Government was directed to constitute an expert committee to examine whether segmentation of national highway projects exceeding 100 kilometres is permissible and, if so, in what circumstances.
issues.legal_principle: Environmental-clearance requirements cannot be defeated by dividing a project into packages below the relevant length threshold. At the same time, the Court did not decide that segmentation is impermissible in every circumstance; it held that the circumstances in which segmentation may be permissible require expert examination. The Court applied the principle that development and environmental protection must proceed together, relying on Indian Council for Enviro-Legal Action v. Union of India and Vellore Citizens’ Welfare Forum v. Union of India.

rule.if: national_highway_expansion_project and project_exceeds_100_km and project_split_into_shorter_packages and split_used_to_evade_clearance

predicates.national_highway_expansion_project: The project proponent undertook an expansion of a national highway.
predicates.project_exceeds_100_km: The overall highway expansion exceeded 100 kilometres.
predicates.project_split_into_shorter_packages: The overall project was divided into separate packages, each shorter than the overall project.
predicates.split_used_to_evade_clearance: The division into packages was used as a strategy to avoid an environmental-clearance requirement.

issues.definition: If a national highway expansion exceeding 100 kilometres is split into shorter packages to avoid environmental clearance, that segmentation is not permitted.

issues.legal_issue: The right of way for a highway project includes the existing highway and the additional land required for the project, including land for toll plazas and rest areas.
material_facts: The proponent argued that toll plazas and rest areas were amenities that should not count toward the right of way.
The Manual of Specifications and Standards described the right of way as the total land width required for the project highway and its associated components.
The Manual’s toll-plaza layout included toll plazas within the right of way.
issues.conclusion: The right of way includes the existing national highway and the land acquired for additional right of way; toll plazas and rest areas are included in that measure.
issues.legal_principle: The Court relied on paragraph 2.3 and the toll-plaza layout in the Manual of Specifications and Standards for Two-Laning of Highways through Public Private Partnership. The right of way is the total land width required for the project highway and its associated facilities, rather than only the land used for the carriageway.

predicates.national_highway_project: The project proponent undertook a project involving a national highway.
predicates.project_requires_associated_facilities: The project required associated facilities such as toll plazas or rest areas.

issues.definition: For a national highway project requiring associated facilities, the right of way includes the existing highway, additional project land, and those facilities.

issues.legal_issue: A highway project involving tree felling must meet the applicable reafforestation requirements.
material_facts: The High Court had raised concerns about the proponent’s compliance with reafforestation undertakings in earlier projects.
The Court noted an obligation to plant ten trees for each tree felled and directed the proponent to fulfil reafforestation requirements under the existing legal regime.
issues.conclusion: The proponent was directed to fulfil the reafforestation requirements under the existing legal regime.
issues.legal_principle: The Court required compliance with the existing legal regime governing reafforestation and noted the obligation to plant ten trees for each tree felled.

predicates.highway_project: The project proponent undertook a highway project.
predicates.trees_felled_for_project: Trees were felled for the highway project.

issues.definition: When trees are felled for a highway project, the applicable reafforestation requirements must be fulfilled.
